strengths: Addresses a clear and useful research question — which embedding space is best for contrastive learning in REC — with a simple, general answer that is convincingly supported by experiments.

C-REX is genuinely a plug-in module: consistent improvements are demonstrated on three distinct REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) and two backbones (Swin-T, Swin-B), which strengthens the generality claim within the primary task.

Well-designed ablations: Table 3 isolates image-text vs image-space vs their combination; Table 4a compares positive-selection strategies; Table 4b isolates the effect of the proposed modified supervised contrastive loss (L*_sup); Table 5a evaluates robustness to paraphrased referring expressions; Table 5b contextualizes the method against a foundation VLM (Molmo).
The paper is well-written and well-organized, with figures (Figs. 1–3) that clearly convey the intuition about text–image misalignment and the scarcity of negative REs.

Reproducibility is good: publicly released checkpoints and official implementations are used where available, training hyperparameters and evaluation protocols are described, and the density-map generation procedure is given in the supplement.
The authors honestly report failure cases (Fig. 8) and mixed results on class-agnostic counting rather than overclaiming, which aids the reader's assessment of the method's scope.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest. The core technical contribution is a supervised contrastive loss (Khosla et al., 2020) adapted to visual tokens, with positives/negatives defined by bipartite matching against ground-truth points. The main insight — moving contrastive supervision from the image-text space to the image space — is essentially a design/ablation finding rather than a new algorithmic component.

The generality claim to class-agnostic counting is only partially supported. Table 2 shows inconsistent improvements: e.g., GroundingREC + C-REX is actually worse than GroundingREC on FSC-147 test MAE (10.12 → 12.46), and CAD-GD regresses on the validation set (13.80 → 13.86). This weakens the 'versatile and general framework' framing.

In Table 1, C-REX does not always surpass the CAD-GD† variant that selects positives via a density-map-based strategy (e.g., Swin-T val: CAD-GD† 4.65 vs CAD-GD + C-REX 4.70; Swin-B val: 4.40 vs 4.38). Since C-REX and CAD-GD† both change the way positives are determined, the paper should clarify how much of the improvement is attributable to the contrastive objective per se versus the token-selection/thresholding strategy, and whether the two are complementary.

The theoretical argument that image-space CL should outperform image-text CL relies on an analogy to DINOv2 vs CLIP performance on smaller datasets, which is not directly established for the REC setting. The claim that text–image alignment is 'typically poor' is asserted rather than empirically quantified on REC-8K.

There is a potential circularity/chicken-and-egg issue: positives are determined by bipartite matching between predicted locations and GT points, so early-training mislocalization could reinforce incorrect positive assignments. No analysis of training dynamics or sensitivity to this effect is provided.
The main paper does not discuss limitations or broader societal implications; these appear only implicitly in the supplementary failure-case figure.

strengths: The paper asks a clean, well-motivated question — which embedding space should be used for contrastive learning in REC — and gives a simple, convincing answer: the image/visual space. The diagnosis of why image–text CL is fragile for REC (poor alignment, and a negative pool limited to the handful of REs available per image, typically <4) is clearly argued and directly motivates the proposed design.

The core contribution, C-REX, is a genuinely plug-in module: it replaces the image–text contrastive loss of existing REC models with an image-space supervised contrastive objective without architectural changes. This makes the work easy to adopt and easy to evaluate fairly.

The empirical evidence is broad and consistent. On REC-8K, C-REX improves three different architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and a GroundingDINO detection baseline) under both Swin-T and Swin-B backbones, e.g. GrDINO MAE 5.92 → 4.26 and RMSE 17.09 → 12.89 on the validation set, with matching F1 gains. The abstract's 'up to 28% MAE / 24.5% RMSE' claim is supported by the numbers in Table 1.

The ablations are informative and well-targeted rather than decorative: Table 3 isolates image–text vs image-space vs their combination (showing image-space alone is best, which is an important control against 'just add another loss'), Table 4a compares positive-sample selection strategies including bipartite matching, and Table 4b isolates the positives-only anchor modification from the vanilla supervised contrastive objective.

The method is shown to be more than a single-dataset trick: it is adapted to class-agnostic counting on FSC-147 and to robustness against paraphrased referring expressions, and is additionally compared against an off-the-shelf VLM (Molmo-2-4B) to show that specialized counting models remain superior — a useful and honest contextualization.

The paper is well written and the figures are effective at conveying the core intuition: Fig. 1/2 make the image–text vs image-space distinction immediately legible, and Fig. 3/4 plus the supplementary qualitative figures (including an explicit failure-case figure) give a good sense of where the gains come from.

Attribution is generally appropriate: the supervised contrastive loss, density-map generation procedure, datasets (REC-8K, FSC-147), backbones (Swin, BERT, GroundingDINO) and baselines are all cited and their protocols described, including the retraining of CAD-GD because no checkpoint was released.

The authors are reasonably candid about limitations: they note that the class-agnostic extension yields smaller gains 'as was expected', that very dense scenes shrink the negative pool, and the supplementary explicitly shows failure cases where C-REX counts confidently but counts the wrong instances.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. The core objective is the supervised contrastive loss of Khosla et al. (2020) applied to visual tokens, with a small change: only positive samples serve as anchors. The justification for that change (negatives lack semantic coherence, so they should not be clustered) is intuitive and verified only empirically via Table 4b; there is no analysis of when/why the modification helps, nor of what the loss converges to.

The generality claim is somewhat overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract and contributions list advertise class-agnostic counting as evidence of versatility, but the FSC-147 results (Table 2) are small and mixed: CAD-GD val MAE 13.80 → 13.86 (worse), GroundingREC test MAE 10.12 → 12.46 (substantially worse), and several RMSE differences are within noise. The 'consistent improvements' phrasing in Section 4.4 does not match the table.

Similarly, the headline REC gains vary widely across configurations. GroundingREC and GroundingDINO improve a lot, but CAD-GD improves only marginally (val 6.33 → 5.98; test 6.25 → 5.97; and CAD-GD† test MAE actually gets worse, 4.81 → 4.61 on MAE but the RMSE/F1 trade-off differs). The paper would be stronger if it explained why the gain is architecture-dependent — e.g. whether it depends on the quality of the bipartite matching, the number of unmatched tokens, or the existing counting loss.

No variance or significance is reported anywhere; every number appears to come from a single training run. Given that several claimed improvements (particularly on FSC-147 and for CAD-GD on REC-8K) are on the order of a few percent of MAE/RMSE, it is hard to tell signal from run-to-run noise.

Key hyperparameters and design choices are not reported in the main paper: the temperature τ, the weighting between the contrastive term and the existing counting losses, whether the contrastive term is applied at every layer/token set, and how the loss behaves early in training when bipartite matching is poor and the 'positive' tokens are therefore unreliable. The interaction with the pre-existing counting loss weight is not ablated at all.

There is no deeper analysis of the mechanism. The paper asserts that image-space CL yields 'more compact intra-class clusters and clearer inter-class separation' (Fig. 2) but never quantifies this (e.g., no embedding-space metrics, no analysis of how the negative pool size correlates with the gain, no study of the dense-scene regime where the negative pool collapses other than a qualitative remark). A quantitative test of the stated hypothesis would substantially strengthen the paper.

The claim that a large negative pool drives the improvement is not fully isolated from the claim that removing image–text misalignment drives it. Table 3 shows image-space CL alone beats image–text CL alone, but there is no control that uses image–text CL with a comparably large negative pool (e.g. all tokens vs all text tokens), so the two hypothesized causes are entangled.

Some presentation and reproducibility details are thin: the 'Project Page' placeholder is empty in the submission, there is no stated code release, and the reference list contains minor inconsistencies in author/venue formatting. The main text defers important training details (density-map procedure, some schedules) to the supplementary.

strengths: Simple, clean, plug-in formulation: C-REX replaces the image-text contrastive loss in existing REC architectures with an image-space supervised contrastive loss and produces consistent, non-trivial gains on REC-8K across three different backbones/architectures (e.g., GroundingREC 6.80 → 4.74 MAE, GroundingDINO 5.92 → 4.26 MAE on the val set).
The design choice to use only positive samples as anchors (Eq. 2) is a sensible fix to the standard SupCon objective in this setting, and Table 4b at least provides some evidence for it.

The paper includes useful ablations: image-text vs. image-space vs. both (Table 3), and positive-selection strategy (top-5, top-N, top-N+√N, bipartite matching) in Table 4a, which supports the bipartite-matching choice.
The extension to class-agnostic counting (FSC-147) demonstrates the framework is not REC-specific, and the qualitative figures and failure-case analysis (Fig. 8) are informative.
Writing is generally clear and the positioning against REC, CAC, ReID, and counting-VQA work is reasonable.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Image-space supervised contrastive learning with bipartite-matched positives is essentially SupCon applied to visual tokens; the paper itself acknowledges that image-space CL has already been used extensively in ReID and segmentation, so the contribution is largely the transfer of an existing technique to a new task rather than a new method.

The central hypothesis — that image-text embedding misalignment is the source of the problem — is asserted rather than demonstrated. There is no diagnostic measurement of image-text alignment quality, no analysis of the geometry of the learned embeddings, and no experiment that isolates the 'misalignment' explanation from the much simpler alternative that C-REX simply adds more/stronger supervision (many more negatives and an auxiliary loss).

Results are mixed and the headline numbers are cherry-picked. CAD-GD† + C-REX is worse on val MAE (4.65 → 4.70) and val RMSE (12.87 → 13.78) in Table 1; in Table 2 (class-agnostic counting) GroundingREC + C-REX is substantially worse on the test set (MAE 10.12 → 12.46). The abstract's 'up to 28% in MAE and 24.5% in RMSE' is the best-case GrDINO val result and is not representative of the paper's overall improvements.

Evaluation is thin: REC results are only on REC-8K and class-agnostic results only on FSC-147, with no variance or significance statistics across runs, making it hard to judge whether the smaller gains (e.g., CAD-GD) are meaningful.

Several claims are unsupported by the presented experiments: the 'efficiency' advantage of image-space CL is asserted but never measured; the statement that dense scenes do not degrade performance ('we do not observe a negative effect') is not backed by an explicit experiment; the claim that C-REX scales better with larger visual backbones is speculative.

The modified SupCon loss (L*_sup) is presented as an important contribution, but the ablation in Table 4b shows identical test RMSE (17.53) between L_sup and L*_sup, weakening the strength of this claim.

The title poses a broad scientific question ('What is the Right Embedding Space?') but the analysis delivered is primarily empirical and intuitive; the paper does not provide the kind of systematic study the framing promises, and the answer ('image space') is largely predictable from prior work in ReID/segmentation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation that converting open-set detectors (Grounding DINO) into centroid predictors is the key factor behind recent detection-based counting success; this insight is validated in Table 6 and used to build a strong baseline.

The proposed C-REX method is simple, clean, and reasonably well-motivated: operating contrastively in image space avoids image-text misalignment and enables a much larger pool of negatives than text-based CL approaches (e.g., Dai et al.).
Strong empirical results on REC-8K, achieving 5.06 MAE / 17.53 RMSE on the test split, which is a substantial improvement over GroundingREC (6.50/19.79) and their improved baseline (5.90/19.73).

Thorough ablation studies: Table 4 justifies the modified supervised contrastive loss (anchors restricted to positives), Table 5 justifies top-N selection, and Table 6 decomposes the contributions of centroid prediction, feature fusion, and CL.

Good qualitative analysis (Figures 2, 3, 4, and supplementary Figure 5) showing that C-REX improves particularly on action, orientation, and location attributes, which aligns with the intended benefit of contrastive learning.
Demonstrated versatility via an adaptation to class-agnostic counting on FSC-147 and CARPK, with competitive results on FSC-147.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty (image-space supervised contrastive learning with top-N positive selection) is modest. Much of the REC improvement over GroundingREC appears to come from the simpler centroid-prediction baseline change rather than the contrastive loss (6.50 → 5.90 from baseline, 5.90 → 5.06 from C-REX), so the incremental value of the CL component is somewhat smaller than the abstract's framing suggests.

The abstract/conclusion claims of 'outperforming previous works by more than 22% in MAE' are technically consistent but potentially misleading, since most of that gain is attributable to the baseline design, not the proposed CL contribution. The relative improvement of C-REX over the paper's own strong baseline is closer to ~14% MAE.

The F1 improvement on REC-8K is very small (0.68 → 0.70 over GroundingREC, 0.68 → 0.70 over the improved baseline), suggesting that the discriminative capacity of the model for correct-instance selection is only marginally improved by the proposed CL loss; this weakens the central narrative that CL is the key driver of better counting.
Only a single REC benchmark (REC-8K) is used, which limits the generality claims for REC. No evaluation on other referring/attribute-counting datasets is provided.

The class-agnostic counting claim is overstated: on CARPK, C-REX (4.21 MAE) is clearly worse than the paper's own improved GDino baseline (3.80 MAE), and the paper does not deeply explain why CL hurts here or how to fix it.

The top-N similarity-based positive selection is somewhat self-referential: positives are the tokens most similar to the masked referring expression, so the contrastive objective partly reinforces the similarity ranking used to define the labels. The justification via ~80% selection accuracy is only a coarse empirical check.

No analysis of training-time cost / batch size requirements is provided, even though the claimed advantage over image-text CL is the ability to leverage many negatives; this advantage is asserted rather than measured.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper. The REC problem setting and the difficulty of distinguishing visually similar objects with different referring expressions is articulated well, and the paper is easy to follow.

The analysis of recent detection-based counting methods (CountGD, GroundingREC) identifying the conversion of open-set detectors from bounding-box to object-centroid predictors as the key driver of their success is a useful, actionable insight. It is validated by the ablation in Table 6, and it is used productively to design a strong baseline.

The design choice to perform contrastive learning entirely in image space (rather than image-text) is sensibly justified: it avoids image-text embedding misalignment and yields a much larger pool of negative samples (hundreds of image tokens vs. a handful of referring expressions). This is a reasonable and defensible argument.

The modified supervised contrastive loss that uses only positive samples as anchors (L*_sup) is well-motivated (the negative class is heterogeneous) and is directly ablated in Table 4, showing a clear gain over both the unmodified loss and the baseline.

Strong and clear state-of-the-art results on REC-8K (test MAE 5.06 / RMSE 17.53 / F1 0.70), supported by a thorough ablation suite (loss modification, number of selections, key baseline components) and compelling qualitative comparisons (Figs. 2, 5, 6, 7).
The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations, including weaker class-agnostic performance on CARPK, and includes honest qualitative failure cases in the supplementary.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The proposed C-REX is essentially a composition of existing ingredients: a Grounding DINO backbone, a supervised contrastive loss, and a top-N similarity-based positive selection heuristic. The headline 'insight' (predicting centroids instead of boxes is better for counting) is fairly intuitive, and the CL module itself is a relatively small modification of an existing loss.

Framing concern / overstatement of the CL contribution. The abstract and introduction emphasize '22% improvement in MAE and >10% in RMSE', but these figures are computed relative to GroundingREC (6.50 MAE), whereas the non-contrastive 'GDino improved' baseline already reaches 5.90 MAE. The contrastive module contributes roughly 14% relative improvement over the paper's own baseline. The framing attributes most of the gain to contrastive learning when a substantial share comes from the baseline change.

The 'general and versatile' claim is not adequately supported. On FSC-147 (Table 2) C-REX is worse than its own baseline on the validation split (10.19 vs 9.71 MAE), and on CARPK (Table 3) it is worse than both its baseline (4.21 vs 3.80 MAE) and CountGD. Calling this 'competitive'/'on par' overstates the evidence; the class-agnostic extension is a third contribution that is only weakly demonstrated.

The top-N positive-selection strategy uses the ground-truth count N to define the number of positives. While defensible at training time, this ties the selection to the very quantity being predicted, and the paper provides only empirical justification (Section 6) without analysis of how errors in the similarity ranking propagate to the learned representation. The 'approximately 80% correct' figure also implies a non-trivial fraction of mislabeled positives whose effect is not quantified.

No statistical evidence for the reported gains: results appear to be single runs with no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing, which matters given the relatively small deltas between C-REX and the improved baseline on some metrics (e.g., F1 and RMSE).

Some implementation details are under-specified for reproducibility: it is not fully clear which modules are frozen vs. finetuned, how the referring-expression class token is masked to form t_m, and how the top-N selection interacts with the 900-token / thresholding scheme. Code is promised but not available at review time, so reproducibility cannot yet be verified.

Minor presentation issues: the C-REX acronym is expanded inconsistently ('REferring' vs 'Referring'), and the class-agnostic adaptation is described in only a few sentences, leaving the adaptation mechanism (positive selection based on class similarity) insufficiently detailed.

strengths: The paper isolates a genuinely useful empirical observation for the counting community: converting an open-set detector (Grounding DINO) into a centroid predictor, with only an L1 point-regression and a classification loss, already outperforms the previously published GroundingREC on REC-8K (5.90 vs 6.50 MAE, 19.73 vs 19.79 RMSE; Tables 1 and 6), showing that GroundingREC's feature-fusion and text-image contrastive modules are not necessary for its accuracy.

The proposed contrastive objective does deliver consistent gains relative to the authors' own baseline, and this is supported by a reasonable set of ablations: the loss form (Table 4), the number of selected positives (Table 5), and the removal of backbone components (Table 6), plus per-count-range (Fig. 3) and per-attribute-category (Fig. 4) breakdowns that show the improvements are not confined to a single bin or attribute type.

The headline REC-8K result (5.06 MAE / 17.53 RMSE / 0.70 F1) is state of the art with a non-trivial relative margin over the previous method (~22% MAE, ~11% RMSE), code is promised, and the qualitative analysis (Figs. 2, 6, 7) includes explicit failure cases, which is good scientific practice and helps the reader judge where the method breaks.
The method itself is simple, well motivated, and easy to implement on top of an existing detection-based counting pipeline, which lowers the barrier to adoption.

The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, and the task framing (referring expression counting) and the gap it targets (distinguishing visually similar instances of the same class) are clearly explained.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim -- that image-space contrastive learning is preferable to the text-image contrastive learning of Dai et al. [11] -- is not experimentally isolated. No experiment applies GroundingREC's text-image CL loss to the improved centroid-detection baseline. The comparison against GroundingREC therefore conflates a backbone/loss change with a CL-loss change, and Section 3.4's argument for image-space CL rests entirely on citations and qualitative reasoning rather than a controlled experiment. This is the single most important missing ablation for the stated contribution.

The 'novel' contrastive loss (Eq. 4) is essentially the standard supervised contrastive loss of Khosla et al. [24] restricted to positive anchors; the only substantive change is that anchors in the negative set are excluded. The normalizer 1/(|I+| - 1) is constant per image and therefore contributes only a per-image additive constant to each term, so it does not constitute a real modification. As written, Eq. 4 is also ill-defined when an image contains a single target (|I+| = 1): the positive set I+ - {i} is empty and the denominator is zero. The claim of a 'novel contrastive loss' is substantially overstated relative to this.

The claim that C-REX 'operates entirely within the image space' is inaccurate: positive selection relies on the image-text similarity y_i between image tokens and the masked referring-expression embedding t_m (Eqs. 2-3). Only the loss itself is image-space; the pseudo-label signal is still cross-modal. This undermines the paper's central motivation about avoiding image-text misalignment.

The versatility/generality claim is contradicted by the authors' own results. On CARPK (Table 3) C-REX (4.21 MAE / 6.12 RMSE) is clearly worse than their own baseline GDino improved (3.80 / 5.16) and worse than CountGD (3.83 / 5.41); on FSC-147 it is far from state of the art (10.19 / 101.46 test vs CountGD's 6.75 / 43.65), and its validation RMSE is worse than the baseline's (57.14 vs 55.11). The abstract's claim of 'strong performance in class-agnostic counting' and the 'on par with the best' framing are not supported by these numbers.

The positive-selection rule uses the ground-truth object count N, i.e., supervision on exactly the quantity being predicted, at training time. The justification offered in Section 4.5.2 and the supplementary is hand-wavy: the claimed '~80% of selected samples correspond to correct instances' is asserted without any measurement or supporting analysis, and the loss/selection scheme cannot be applied where counts are unavailable, which directly limits the claimed generality.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the temperature tau, batch size, number of training epochs, and hardware are not reported, and 'image tokens' (which tokens of the DETR/Grounding DINO pipeline are contrasted) are never precisely defined. Given that the C-REX-vs-baseline gap is only ~0.8 MAE on the test set, the absence of multiple seeds, error bars, or any significance analysis is a material concern; the size of the REC-8K test split is also never stated.

Evaluation breadth is thin for the headline claim: the main REC result rests on a single dataset (REC-8K). The class-agnostic extension is evaluated on two datasets, but the improvement there is marginal on FSC-147 and negative on CARPK, so the 'general and versatile' framing is not earned.

There are framing and table-consistency issues that suggest selective reporting: e.g., Table 2's caption states all models are trained on FSC-147 while CountGD's much stronger numbers come from multi-dataset training; Table 1's 'GDino' row and Tables 2/3's 'GDino impr.' row are not clearly reconciled; and the abstract's '22% MAE / 10% RMSE' figures are relative improvements over one prior method on one dataset, which reads as more impressive than the absolute 6.50 -> 5.06 MAE change warrants.
